title: Causal reasoning and correlation
note: A correlation means two variables tend to move together. It is evidence about causes, not proof: the pattern may come from chance, reverse causation, or a confounder that drives both. Mill's methods find causes by comparing cases: what all cases of the effect share, what differs between cases with and without it, and what varies in step with it. Randomized experiments cut the link to confounders.

read.title: From pattern to cause
text: Ice cream sales and drownings rise and fall together. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. Hot weather sends more people to buy ice cream and more people into the water. Hot weather is a confounder, a third factor that drives both variables. Correlations can also arise from chance, especially when many variables are searched, or from reverse causation, where the supposed effect is really the cause.

John Stuart Mill described methods for moving from patterns to causes. The method of agreement looks for the one factor shared by every case of the effect, such as the one dish all sick diners ate. The method of difference compares cases that are alike except for one factor; if the effect appears only where the factor does, that factor is part of the cause. Concomitant variation tracks whether the effect grows and shrinks with a factor.

Mill's methods are only as good as our list of candidate factors. A hidden factor can fool any of them. That is why randomized experiments are so valuable: by assigning treatment by chance, they spread confounders evenly across groups, so a difference in outcome points to the treatment itself.
